基本操作為取兩把湯匙，以匙面互相敲擊發聲。初學可採火鉗式：兩匙凹面朝外，食指置於: The basic action is to take two spoons and strike the bowls against each other. A beginner can use the fire tongs style: the two spoons with their hollows facing out, the index finger between the handles to leave a gap, then strike the spoons against the knee or the palm. Another, the salad serving style, puts one spoon between little finger, ring finger and middle finger and the other between ring finger, thumb and index finger, turning about the ring finger as axis, and closing middle finger and thumb so that the backs strike. The castanet style holds two spoons in each hand, one with its hollow against the palm and pressed by the thumb, the other gripped between ring and middle fingers, and grips with the middle and ring fingers so that the backs strike. The point of the sound is controlling the gap, the striking faces and the force; different striking points give different rhythms and timbres.

Their use is scattered through European and North American folk music: Russia had wooden spoons, three or more at a time, by at least the 18th century, and they later appeared in folk performance and orchestras; Greece calls them koutalakia (little spoons), and dancers beat time with them, a practice once popular among Anatolian Greeks; Turkey and Uzbekistan call them kaşıklar, commonly of boxwood and held in various ways. In British, American and Canadian folk music the spoons accompany the fiddle and are associated with jug bands, spasm bands and minstrel performance, and they are used in Quebec, Acadia, Newfoundland and Métis culture.
Spoons are an idiophone, Hornbostel-Sachs number 111.141, in the same struck-together family as castanets. The player strikes the hollows or the backs of two or more spoons against each other, and can also use the knee, palm, fingers and other parts of the body to make rhythms. They are used in European and North American folk music: in Britain, Quebec and the Atlantic provinces of Canada they accompany the fiddle, and in the United States they are used in folk music and minstrelsy.
